title: 2 days Upper (Torso/Arm dominant) split program review
summary: Review of a viewer's (Keith) calisthenics-based alternating torso/arm upper split done three times a week with only a pull-up bar, parallettes, rings and dumbbells. He praises the evolving rep ranges that let back-off volume compensate for strength work, critiques static rep ranges on strength movements and the high-rep cheat laterals, explains how to program cheat reps, and suggests supersets and giant sets, more wrist extensions, long-head triceps work, hanging leg raises and some shrugs.

claims.claim: Whatever setup you have, do the best you can with it; calisthenics-only programs are fine.
Static rep schemes like 5x3 mean the first set was too easy; replace them with evolving ranges (e.g. 3 sets of 3-5 or 5 sets of 3-6) that give similar tonnage but make progression easier.
Weighted pull-ups work best in low rep ranges; 4x4-6 is good, and once you hit something like 6,6,6,5 you can add weight.
4x4-6 on weighted dips allows good progression on weighted calisthenics.
Bodyweight pull-ups should be done in higher rep ranges.
Fixed rep ranges are fine for back-off/secondary movements: as your strength work gets heavier, you do the back-off in a more fatigued state, so it stays hard and the point is just to add volume.
He prefers leaning lateral raises to standing cheat laterals because cheating when the body is not upright is less risky and more productive.
Keep cheat reps, especially for small muscles, in lower rep ranges; 4x10 cheat laterals hit the traps a lot and later reps become more of a cheat than early ones.

When cheating, cheat at the same intensity on every rep; the cheat should only bring the weight to the point where the muscle can finish it. Using more body English as the set goes on works the muscle less and is more dangerous.

Evolving rep ranges placed synergistically let volume self-regulate: a weak strength day (5,4,4,4) is made up with more back-off volume, and a great day (6,6,6) still allows the minimum back-off work.
Programs need to be strict but not too strict; leaving room to manipulate volume is both the science and the art.
Pinch grip trains an open-hand grip and different functions than the crush grip used in barbell pulls; people with strong barbell grip can still have weak pinch grip.
He prefers more intense grip work: 4-5 sets of about 15-second holds carry over better and progress faster than 25-second holds.
Rear delts have a striking diminishing return; there's no need to hammer them, especially when cheat laterals already tax them.

Leave heavy strength work un-supersetted, but superset non-overlapping accessories (e.g. pull-ups with laterals, ring rows with ring push-ups, giant set of grip, band curls and rear delt flies) to save time, add cardio stress and raise intensity.
He's cautious with close-grip supinated movements because they stress his bicep tendon; start them with light weight to test range of motion and leverages, and pull with the lats on chin-ups.
Fixed rep ranges suit lifts like triceps-lean dips where you could otherwise cheat via torso angle to hit more reps; stopping at mechanical failure with proper form is better.
Strict curls are a valid compound you can progress with evolving rep ranges, though they are tough to progress on.
He uses push-ups as a bridge for extra chest volume when needed.
Vary pull-up grips; it's underrated. He feels wide grip more in his lats and close grip more in his arms, so he does mostly wide since his arms are already big.
Arms deserve to be babied with lots of volume if you want them to grow.
Heavy pressing and dips develop the lateral and medial triceps heads, so the long head may lag; do extensions with shoulder flexion and slow negatives to feel the stretch.
Curls and chin-ups mostly stimulate the inner forearm, so do more wrist extensions than wrist curls, e.g. 6x12 extensions vs 2x12 curls.
If you don't train legs, use more supersets to compensate for the cardiovascular and caloric benefit you'd otherwise get from leg training.
Without squats, deadlifts or standing presses, add direct ab work such as hanging leg raises, which can be supersetted with almost anything.
Pull-ups hit the traps to an extent but not as effectively as shrugs.

progress by deficit or leg angle

exercises.why: high reps of cheats tax traps and rear delts
